title: Integration: Rome in Our Words, Calendars and Cities
objective: After this level you can trace Rome's legacy in languages, calendars, architecture and city planning.
summary: Roman towns became London and Paris, Roman columns became capitols and banks, and July and August still honor Caesar and Augustus.

cards.headline: You can see Rome in a city map, a bank front and a calendar.
cards.body: The empire is long gone. Its fingerprints aren’t. Let’s go looking for them.

cards.headline: Cities and buildings
cards.body: Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna. Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. Much later, neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas. Next time you pass a bank with columns out front, you’re looking at a Roman idea wearing a suit.

cards.headline: Words and time
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin kept changing until it became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of those Romance languages, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. Now check a calendar. July is named for Julius Caesar, and August for Augustus. Rome’s two most famous names, still sitting side by side every year.

cards.fact: “E pluribus unum”: out of many, one.
cards.context: Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins. This one sits on the Great Seal of the United States: a modern country describing itself in Rome’s language.

cards.headline: The legacy: traced
learned: Many European cities grew from Roman towns
Latin lives on in words and mottoes

questions.prompt: Which of these cities grew from a Roman town?
questions.explanation: London was founded by the Romans; Paris, Cologne and Vienna also grew from Roman towns or forts.

questions.prompt: Why do so many capitols and banks have columns and domes?

options.label: They were built by Roman engineers

questions.explanation: Neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts to borrow Rome’s prestige.

questions.prompt: From Level 48: which month honors Rome’s first emperor?
questions.explanation: Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in 8 BCE.
